subject: Chemistry
title: Oganesson: The Newest Noble Gas
description: A micro-lesson that makes Oganesson: The Newest Noble Gas usable.

hook.text: Element 118 sits at the bottom-right corner of the periodic table. Only a few atoms have ever existed.

buildup.text: Russian and American scientists created it in 2002 by smashing calcium atoms into californium targets.

discovery.text: They named it oganesson after Yuri Oganessian, a living scientist—an extremely rare honor.

twist.text: It's a noble gas on paper, but it probably acts nothing like one. Predictions say it behaves like a solid.

climax.text: It decays in less than a millisecond. We know it exists only from the debris it leaves behind.

punchline.text: The heaviest element. Gone in a millisecond. Noble in name only.

quiz.question: What is unusual about oganesson compared to other noble gases?
options: It may behave like a solid rather than a gas
It is the lightest noble gas
It occurs naturally in volcanic vents

details.summary: Oganesson, element 118, was synthesized in 2002 at Russia's Joint Institute for Nuclear Research and named after nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian..
details.whyItMatters: Oganesson challenges everything we think we know about noble gases. Relativistic effects on its electrons may make it a reactive solid rather than an inert gas, revealing how physics modifies chemistry at extreme atomic numbers.
takeaways: Oganesson is the heaviest element on the periodic table at atomic number 118
Only a handful of atoms have ever been created, each lasting mere milliseconds
Relativistic effects may make it behave entirely unlike other noble gases

faq.question: Why is oganesson expected to behave differently from other noble gases?
faq.answer: At element 118, electrons orbit so fast that relativistic mass increase alters orbital shapes and energies. Calculations suggest oganesson's outer electron shell is so spread out that it cannot maintain the closed-shell stability that makes other noble gases inert..

faq.question: How was oganesson synthesized in the laboratory?
faq.answer: Scientists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research bombarded californium-249 targets with calcium-48 ions accelerated to high energy..
